parts.text: We also found evidence of loss aversion. Students were asked to imagine two coin

, risking £25 on one and £100 on the other, and named the smallest prize that would make each worth playing. Across both flips, around 75% asked for more than they stood to lose (indicating loss aversion),

in line with findings from research involving people in 53 countries.

It would be reassuring to think people studying for a finance masters – several with real trading experience already – would be less susceptible to these bases. Our results suggest

.

That does not prove financial knowledge makes no difference. We did not compare this group with people who had no financial background. And we measured them once, not as their

grew as time progressed.

But it does show that technical, theoretical knowledge of markets was not, by itself, enough to stop these tendencies appearing. These biases are not really about what you know. They are about how the mind processes wins, losses and

, often automatically, before conscious reasoning gets a look in.

So what can investors do?

There was, however, an encouraging sign after a structured
of exercises, comparing predictions against outcomes, reviewing their own trading data and reflecting on decisions. The self-rated understanding of all three biases by students improved

.

It is important to note that this measured how well students felt they understood the biases, not their actual knowledge or behaviour. Feeling more aware of a bias is not the same as reliably avoiding it. As the study itself notes,

is a start, but it doesn’t guarantee different decisions.

None of this means investors are doomed to be led astray by their own

, but simply knowing the theory isn’t enough. What seemed to help our students was structure. In other words, writing down what they expected before deciding, then honestly comparing it with what happened, reviewing their own trading history for patterns rather than
memory, and also setting rules for buying and selling in advance, not in the heat of the moment.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Psychological biases can lead investors to make poor financial decisions.
Consumers' ideas about organic food do not always match what labels and standards communicate.
State responses to childcare funding cuts offer lessons for future policy.
Fireworks create environmental and economic costs that outlast the celebrations.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: Yet there’s been surprisingly little research into teaching students to recognise these biases in their own decisions, rather than just learning the theory.

questions.prompt: Which biases are examined alongside self-attribution?
questions.explanation: 第 4 段提供了作答依据。正确选项用不同说法表达了文中的信息；请比较范围、数量、因果关系与限定词。
questions.evidence: My colleagues and I explore this in our latest study, which examines self-attribution alongside two related biases – overconfidence and loss aversion – among people training to work in finance.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is explicitly made in paragraph 9?
options: This bias matters more now that trading apps have made it easier for people with no formal training in finance to manage their own investments.
Over four weeks, the students learned about trading psychology and then took part in a series of simulated trading exercises.
We studied the financial decisions of 72 postgraduate students taking an MSc in finance and investment at the University of South Wales.
Students were asked to imagine two coin flips, risking £25 on one and £100 on the other, and named the smallest prize that would make each worth playing.
